topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Cardiac monitoring, chest auscultation and neurological observations in children
blurb: Interpret a child's monitor rhythm, recognise key breath sounds on auscultation, and carry out and escalate neurological observations using NICE NG232.
question: Ruby, 3, is on the ward after a head injury. Her GCS has been 14. On her next set of observations her right pupil is larger than her left. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Cardiac monitoring, chest auscultation and neurological observations are Annexe B procedures that children's nurses must perform and interpret. Formally, each turns a physical finding into data that feeds a track and trigger system such as PEWS. Plain English: know what is normal for a child (some findings that would worry you in an adult are normal in children), recognise the danger signs, and escalate quickly when a trend changes.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency Annexe B 2.5, 2.8, 2.12

rows.label: Pattern
values: Rate rises breathing in, falls breathing out
Sudden, very fast, regular, narrow complex

rows.label: Rate variation
values: Fixed, does not vary with activity

rows.label: Response
values: Escalate; 12-lead ECG; vagal manoeuvres if stable

teach.caption: Sinus arrhythmia is common in healthy children and is more obvious at slower rates.

steps.label: Stable
steps.sub: Vagal manoeuvres: modified Valsalva or ice pack to face

steps.label: Adenosine
steps.sub: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg rapid IV flush (max 6 mg), ECG running

teach.caption: In bradycardia with poor perfusion that does not respond to oxygenation and ventilation (HR under 60), start chest compressions.

teach.h: What you hear and what it means
head: Sound
When
Suggests
teach.caption: A quieter chest is not always better: falling wheeze with rising effort or exhaustion means less air is moving.

items: Let the child sit on a parent's lap; explain and warm the stethoscope.
Listen first while the child is calm, before more upsetting checks.
Compare left with right at the same level, front and back.
Use a paediatric-sized stethoscope head on infants for a good seal.
Note work of breathing alongside sounds: rate, recession, nasal flaring.

teach.body: After a head injury, the minimum documented observations are GCS, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation. In preverbal children, use the paediatric GCS with a 'grimace' alternative to the verbal score. Observations are half-hourly until GCS 15, then half-hourly for 2 hours, hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly.

head: Sign of deterioration
rows: Sustained (30 min) drop of 1 GCS point, especially motor
Drop of 3+ in eye or verbal, or 2+ in motor
Severe or increasing headache, or persistent vomiting
New pupil inequality or limb asymmetry
teach.caption: If a child with GCS 15 deteriorates after the first 2 hours, revert to half-hourly observations and restart the schedule (rec 1.9.12).

teach.text: Do not record 'irregular pulse' as an arrhythmia in a well child without watching it against breathing. A rate that speeds up on inspiration and slows on expiration is sinus arrhythmia, which is normal in children. A fast, fixed, regular rate that does not change is the worrying pattern.

teach.body: Ruby's GCS has been 14. At her next check, nurse Femi finds her right pupil larger than her left. This is new pupil inequality, an NG232 sign of neurological deterioration. Femi calls the doctor immediately for urgent reassessment, increases observations, keeps Ruby's airway safe, and uses ISBAR to hand over the change and the trend.

items: Sinus arrhythmia (rate varies with breathing) is normal in children.
Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine 0.1–0.2 mg/kg (max 6 mg); unstable: synchronised cardioversion.
Stridor = upper airway; wheeze = lower airway; grunting and silent chest are danger signs.
Neuro obs: GCS (grimace for preverbal), pupils, limbs plus vital signs; half-hourly until GCS 15.
New pupil inequality, a sustained 1-point GCS drop or worsening headache needs urgent reassessment.

summary: You can now tell normal sinus arrhythmia from SVT and know the first steps for SVT, interpret stridor, wheeze, crackles, grunting and a silent chest, and carry out neurological observations to NG232. You can also recognise the changes that need urgent reassessment.

A.q: Ruby, 3, has a head injury. Her GCS has been 14. On her next observations her right pupil is larger than her left. What should the nurse do?
options: Document it and continue the schedule
Dim the lights and recheck in 30 minutes
A.why: NG232: new pupil inequality is a sign of neurological deterioration that needs urgent reassessment.

whyNot.0: Waiting an hour delays action on a sign of rising intracranial pressure.
whyNot.2: Documenting without escalating misses a key deterioration sign.
whyNot.3: Changing lighting and rechecking delays escalation of a new asymmetry.

A.q: Leo, 6, is on a cardiac monitor. His heart rate rises to 110 when he breathes in and falls to 85 when he breathes out. He is well. What is this most likely to be?
A.why: A heart rate that rises on inspiration and falls on expiration is sinus arrhythmia, a normal finding in children.

whyNot.0: SVT is a fast, fixed, regular rate that does not vary with breathing.
whyNot.1: Heart block causes slow rates and dropped or dissociated beats, not breathing-linked variation.
whyNot.3: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular and not linked to the breathing cycle.

A.q: Aiden, 2, has a barking cough. The nurse hears a high-pitched noise when he breathes in. What does this suggest?
A.why: Stridor is a high-pitched inspiratory sound from narrowing of the upper airway, typical of croup.

whyNot.0: Lower airway narrowing produces mainly expiratory wheeze.
whyNot.2: Fluid in the alveoli produces crackles.
whyNot.3: A pleural rub is a creaking sound with breathing, not a high-pitched inspiratory noise.

B.q: Noah, 4 months, is feeding poorly. His monitor shows a narrow complex tachycardia at 270 beats/min that does not vary. He is pink, alert and well perfused. What is the first-line treatment?
B.why: RCUK 2025: for narrow complex SVT without decompensated circulatory failure, consider vagal manoeuvres such as an ice pack to the face, then IV adenosine.

whyNot.0: Synchronised cardioversion is for SVT with decompensated circulatory failure.
whyNot.2: Amiodarone is not first line for stable SVT.
whyNot.3: Compressions are for cardiac arrest or bradycardia with poor perfusion.

B.q: Ava, 7, has a head injury and her GCS has been 15 since arrival. What is the minimum observation frequency for the first 6 hours?
options: Every 15 minutes for the first 6 hours
B.why: NG232 rec 1.9.11: with GCS 15, half-hourly for 2 hours, then hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly.

whyNot.0: Hourly misses the half-hourly checks needed in the first 2 hours.
whyNot.2: 2-hourly is the frequency after the first 6 hours.
whyNot.3: 15-minute observations are not the NG232 schedule for GCS 15.

B.q: Toby, 14 months, is observed after a fall from a sofa. He babbles but has no words. How should his verbal response be assessed?
options: Score verbal as 1 because he has no words yet
Use the adult GCS and note his age
Use the paediatric GCS grimace alternative
B.why: NG232 rec 1.3.4: the paediatric GCS includes a 'grimace' alternative to the verbal score so preverbal children can be scored.

whyNot.0: Scoring 1 would wrongly suggest no response and distort the GCS.
whyNot.1: A blank score loses the information the GCS needs.
whyNot.2: The adult verbal score cannot be applied to a preverbal child.

C.q: Jess, 8, has acute asthma. Earlier, wheeze was heard throughout her chest. Now she is too breathless to talk, her wheeze has almost gone and air entry is poor. What does this indicate?
options: She needs a repeat peak flow
Her inhaler has started to work
C.why: A silent chest with poor air entry is a life-threatening feature: so little air is moving that wheeze can no longer be heard.

whyNot.0: Less wheeze with worsening breathlessness is deterioration, not improvement.
whyNot.2: Peak flow should not delay emergency treatment in life-threatening asthma.
whyNot.3: Treatment response would bring easier breathing and better air entry, not a silent chest.

C.q: Sam, 10, is on 2-hourly head injury observations with GCS 15. At 8 hours his GCS falls to 14 and stays there for 30 minutes. What should happen?
options: Wait to see if it falls further
C.why: A sustained 1-point drop is a sign of deterioration (rec 1.9.13), and NG232 rec 1.9.12 says revert to half-hourly observations and restart the schedule.

whyNot.0: Continuing 2-hourly checks ignores a sustained drop in GCS.
whyNot.1: NG232 reverts to half-hourly, not hourly, with urgent reassessment.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a further fall delays treatment of possible intracranial bleeding.

C.q: Ellie, 3 months, has bronchiolitis. The nurse hears a short noise at the end of each breath out and sees marked recession. What should the nurse do?
options: Suction and recheck in an hour
Record it as a normal infant breathing pattern
C.why: Grunting is a sign of severe respiratory distress; it is a red feature in NG143 and a 999 criterion in bronchiolitis (NG9).

whyNot.1: Suction alone and a delayed recheck do not address severe distress.
whyNot.2: Grunting is a sign of severe respiratory distress, not a normal infant breathing pattern.
whyNot.3: Salbutamol is not used in bronchiolitis (NG9).

reteach.title: Normal for a child, worrying for an adult
reteach.question: Which findings look alarming but are normal in children, and which look small but are dangerous?

blocks.body: Some findings are normal in children: a heart rate that rises and falls with breathing (sinus arrhythmia) and higher resting rates than adults. Others look small but are danger signs: a single new unequal pupil, a 1-point GCS drop that lasts 30 minutes, grunting, or a chest that goes quiet while the child works harder to breathe.

blocks.text: Hypotension and bradycardia are late signs in children. Act on changes in behaviour, breathing and perfusion before the blood pressure falls.

explain.body: Sinus arrhythmia: rate rises on inspiration, falls on expiration; normal in children. SVT: sudden, very fast, regular, narrow complex; needs urgent review.

test.q: What must be running while adenosine is given for SVT in a child?
test.why: RCUK 2025: ensure a 12-lead ECG is running during adenosine administration.

whyNot.1: An arterial line is not required to give adenosine.
whyNot.2: An EEG records brain activity, not the heart rhythm response.
whyNot.3: Capnography monitors ventilation, not the rhythm change.

explain.body: Stridor: inspiratory, upper airway. Wheeze: mainly expiratory, lower airway. Crackles: fluid or secretions. Grunting: severe distress. Silent chest: life-threatening asthma.

test.q: Which sound mainly heard on expiration suggests narrowing of the lower airways?
test.why: Wheeze is a musical, mainly expiratory sound from narrowed lower airways.

whyNot.0: Stridor is inspiratory and comes from the upper airway.
whyNot.1: Grunting is a short expiratory noise of severe distress, not airway narrowing.
whyNot.2: A pleural rub comes from inflamed pleura.

explain.body: Minimum: GCS, pupil size and reactivity, limb movements, RR, HR, BP, temperature and SpO2. Paediatric GCS uses a grimace alternative for preverbal children.

test.q: Which observation is part of the NG232 minimum neurological observations after head injury?
test.why: NG232 rec 1.9.10 lists GCS, pupils, limb movements, RR, HR, BP, temperature and SpO2.

whyNot.0: Glucose is useful but not in the listed minimum.
whyNot.1: Peak flow is a respiratory measure, not a neuro observation.
whyNot.3: Urine output is not in the NG232 minimum list.

explain.body: Urgent reassessment for agitation, a sustained 1-point GCS drop, a 3-point eye or verbal or 2-point motor drop, severe or increasing headache, persistent vomiting, or new pupil or limb asymmetry.

test.q: Which change after a head injury needs urgent reassessment under NG232?
test.why: Persistent vomiting is listed as a sign of neurological deterioration needing urgent reassessment.

whyNot.1: A single episode of crying is not a listed deterioration sign.
whyNot.2: Asking for a drink is normal behaviour.
whyNot.3: Normal sleep is expected; observations continue but it is not deterioration.
